solution.concept_anchor: Structural causes of Eka movement emergence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may choose option (a) because Kisan Sabhas are correctly associated with Awadh and their role as a precursor to Eka is well-known — but the question asks what 'most directly' caused Eka to emerge separately, and the answer is the Kisan Sabha's failure to represent lower castes and bargadars, not its mere existence.
elimination_logic: Eliminate the 'existence of Kisan Sabhas' as the cause — it was the Kisan Sabha's upper-peasant bias and failure to represent lower castes that drove Eka, not the Kisan Sabha's existence per se.
Eliminate 'Gandhi's personal directive to form a separate lower-caste movement' — Gandhi did not direct Eka's formation; the movement was autonomous of Gandhi and Congress.

The structural cause is the Kisan Sabha's failure to represent bargadars and lower-caste tenants combined with the immediate triggers of excessive rent and illegal levies — option (c) captures this correctly.

Confirm option (c): The combination of the Kisan Sabha's upper-peasant bias leaving lower castes underrepresented, and the persistence of excessive rents and illegal exactions, is the correct structural explanation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (a) almost gives the right answer — Kisan Sabha involvement IS relevant to Eka's genesis, but it was specifically the Kisan Sabha's failure (its upper-peasant bias) rather than its existence that explains why Eka emerged separately. Students who remember 'Kisan Sabha' as connected to Eka without knowing the precise causal mechanism (the Sabha's exclusion of lower castes) will gravitate toward option (a). The distinction between a precursor organisation's existence and its specific failure is the pivot.
solution.final_explanation:
The Eka movement emerged not in isolation but as a response to a specific combination of structural failures — both within the peasant movement itself and in the colonial agrarian system.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Kisan Sabha's mere existence was not the cause. It was the Kisan Sabha's failure to represent lower-caste tenants and bargadars — its upper-peasant bias — that created the social demand for Eka. Framing it as 'existence' rather than 'failure' is a subtle but important distortion.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Gandhi issued no directive for a separate lower-caste movement. Eka was entirely autonomous — Madari Pasi organised it from below without any directive from national Congress leadership.
• Option (c) — Correct: The convergence of the Kisan Sabha's upper-peasant bias (excluding lower castes and bargadars) with the persistence of excessive rents 50% above recorded rates, nazrana demands, and begar — even after the Oudh Rent Amendment Act's partial concessions — is the correct structural explanation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While post-WWI agrarian distress was a background condition, it affected all peasant groups equally. The specific reason Eka emerged separately was the Kisan Sabha's social exclusion of lower castes — the distress alone does not explain Eka's distinct social character.

Value Addition:
• The pattern of lower-caste peasants forming separate movements when upper-caste organisations fail to represent them repeats in other contexts — e.g., Ambedkar's critique of Congress's peasant organisations.
• 'Upper-peasant bias' in movement leadership is a recurring theme in subaltern studies analysis of Indian agrarian movements.
• The Eka movement demonstrates that 'agrarian unrest' is not monolithic — different caste-class positions within the peasantry produce different organisational forms.

concepts_used: Religious and Syncretic Elements in Eka Mobilisation
The 'Eka' Oath Ritual: Content, Symbolism, and Significance

solution.concept_anchor: Religious idiom in Eka — mobilisation tool and class limitation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that religious idiom was used by Eka AND that it helped mobilise illiterate peasants (making R seem to explain A) will choose (a). The trap is that A claims the idiom 'constrained' secular articulation, and R explains why it was used (effective mobilisation) — but R explains the choice of idiom, not the constraint.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Marxist and secular historiographical accounts both note that the religious framing of Eka's resistance, while effective for mobilisation, limited the movement's ability to articulate a class-secular agrarian programme — the idiom that enabled mobilisation also constrained the ideological horizon.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Using religious symbols and oath-rituals was an effective mobilisation tool among largely illiterate peasant communities who responded to sacred commitments — this is well-documented.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R explains WHY religious idiom was used (effectiveness). A claims the religious idiom constrained class-secular articulation. These are two different claims: one about the utility of religious idiom (R), one about its limiting effect (A). R does not explain why the idiom constrained articulation; it explains why the idiom was adopted. The causal explanation of A requires the additional step that religious framing displaced class framing — which R does not provide.
Both A and R are correct, R does not explain A — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a subtle reversed-causation trap. A and R are both correct, and they concern the same phenomenon (religious idiom). But A addresses the constraining effect of religious idiom on class articulation, while R addresses the enabling effect of religious idiom on peasant mobilisation. These are not cause-effect but two sides of the same coin. Students who read both as 'about religious idiom' will accept R as explaining A. The precise causal analysis requires distinguishing between 'why idiom was used' (R) and 'what effect the idiom had on ideological range' (A).
solution.final_explanation:
The religious idiom of the Eka movement — sacred water oaths, syncretic Hindu-Muslim rituals — was simultaneously the movement's greatest organisational strength and its ideological limitation.

• Assertion (A): Correct. While effective for mobilisation, the religious framing of Eka's resistance meant its demands were articulated in terms of sacred obligations and moral economy rather than class rights and agrarian transformation. This limited the movement's ability to develop a class-secular programme — a critique emphasised in Marxist historiography.
• Reason (R): Correct. Indigenous religious symbols and oath-rituals were the most effective mobilisation tools available among largely illiterate rural communities in Awadh, where sacred commitments carried greater binding force than formal contracts or written pledges.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. R explains the strategic rationale for using religious idiom (it worked as a mobilisation tool). A claims that this same idiom constrained the movement's ideological horizon. These are two independent observations about the same phenomenon — the causal explanation of A requires additional reasoning about how religious framing displaces class analysis, which R alone does not provide.

Value Addition:
• The tension between religious idiom and class analysis in peasant movements is a pan-South Asian theme — the Telangana movement (with Communist organisation) is the example of religious idiom being more successfully subordinated to class analysis.
• E.P. Thompson's concept of 'moral economy' — the idea that peasant protest is framed in terms of violated customary rights rather than abstract class interest — is applicable to the Eka case.
• The syncretic character of Eka's religious idiom (Hindu AND Muslim symbols) prevented the religious framing from becoming communally divisive — unlike the Mappila case.

Reason (R): Indigenous religious symbols and sacred oath-rituals carried strong binding force among largely illiterate rural communities in Awadh, where formal contracts or written pledges had little social authority, making religious idiom the most effective available mobilisation tool.

solution.concept_anchor: Nazrana definition and legal status in Awadh tenancy
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Lagaan' (the standard term for rent) is the most familiar Hindi term in the agrarian-legal vocabulary that students know, and they may confuse it with nazrana because both are payments made by tenants to landlords. The crucial distinction is that lagaan is the recorded, legally recognised rent, while nazrana is the extra-legal premium above it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate 'lagaan' — that is the recorded rent itself, legally authorised under tenancy law. Nazrana is the premium above and beyond recorded rent.
Eliminate 'batai' — that refers to the crop-sharing arrangement (sharecropping), not an extra premium payment.
Eliminate 'maalguzari' — that is a land revenue term used in Central Provinces contexts, not the specific Awadh extra-legal premium.
Confirm 'nazrana' — the illegal premium demanded at lease renewal or transfer, unrecognised under tenancy law but extracted through social coercion — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'lagaan' for 'nazrana' — both are tenant payments, but with opposite legal statuses. Lagaan is the legally recorded rent (exactly what Eka demanded be paid — and nothing more). Nazrana is the extra-legal premium above lagaan (exactly what Eka demanded be refused). Students who know Eka resisted 'rent exploitation' without distinguishing between the legal rent and the illegal premium will conflate the two terms and select 'lagaan' as the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the precise vocabulary of Awadh agrarian exploitation is essential for interpreting Eka's demands accurately.

• Option (a) — Correct: Nazrana was the extra-legal premium extracted by zamindars above and beyond the recorded rent (lagaan) at the time of lease renewal or tenancy transfer. It had no recognition under colonial tenancy law but was enforced through social coercion and economic dependency — making it the most visible symbol of arbitrary landlord power and a prime target for Eka's resistance.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Lagaan is the legally recorded rent itself — the amount Eka pledged to pay (at recorded rates only). Confusing nazrana with lagaan inverts the movement's entire legal logic.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Batai refers to the crop-sharing arrangement between landlord and sharecropper — it describes a tenurial relationship, not an extra-legal premium payment.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Maalguzari is a land revenue term from Central Provinces contexts — it refers to the revenue paid by village headmen to the colonial state, not the extra premium in Awadh's tenancy system.

Value Addition:
• Nazrana could equal 6–12 months of recorded rent — pushing tenants into mahajan debt bondage to raise the demanded sum.
• Eka's strategic framing — 'we will pay lagaan at recorded rates and refuse nazrana' — was legally astute: it positioned tenants as law-abiding and zamindars as the violators.
• The economic chain from nazrana demand → inability to pay → mahajan loan → debt bondage → de facto permanent tenancy surrender is a documented pattern of colonial Awadh agrarian exploitation.

(a) Nazrana

solution.concept_anchor: Madari Pasi — community, movement, and colonial classification
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Madari Pasi led a peasant movement in Awadh may assume he was from the Chamar community (the most prominently discussed Dalit community in UP), particularly since Chamars also participated in the Eka movement.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Madari Pasi was from the Pasi community, not the Chamar community. Both participated in Eka but the leader was specifically from the Pasi community.
Eliminate option (b) — Madari Pasi led the Eka movement, not the Awadh Kisan Sabha. The Awadh Kisan Sabha was led by Baba Ramchandra.

Confirm option (c) — Madari Pasi was from the Pasi community, which was listed under the Colonial Criminal Tribes Act. This dual marginalisation — as a low-caste tenant AND as a member of a 'criminalised' community — is the key biographical fact.
Eliminate option (d) — Madari Pasi operated in Awadh (United Provinces), not in Punjab or Central Provinces.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates in two directions: (1) substituting 'Chamar' for 'Pasi' (option a) — both are lower-caste communities that participated in Eka, but the leader was Pasi; and (2) substituting 'Awadh Kisan Sabha' for 'Eka movement' (option b) — both were Awadh-based agrarian organisations, but Madari Pasi led Eka, not the Kisan Sabha. Students who know the broad contours (lower-caste leader, Awadh peasant movement) without memorising the specific community name will fall into one of these two traps.
solution.final_explanation:
Madari Pasi's personal profile is historically significant in multiple dimensions — his caste, his colonial classification, and his movement leadership.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Madari Pasi was from the Pasi community, not the Chamar community. While Chamars participated in the Eka movement, the leader was specifically a Pasi — a distinction that matters for understanding the movement's social composition.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Madari Pasi led the Eka movement, not the Awadh Kisan Sabha. Baba Ramchandra led the Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920) — the entity-swap between these two leaders of related but distinct movements is the most common exam confusion in this topic.
• Option (c) — Correct: Madari Pasi was from the Pasi community and this community was listed under the Colonial Criminal Tribes Act — making his leadership doubly politically significant. A member of a 'criminalised' caste led a major agrarian resistance movement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Madari Pasi's activities were in the Awadh region of the United Provinces (present-day Uttar Pradesh), not in Punjab or Central Provinces.

Value Addition:
• The Criminal Tribes Act (1871, amended 1911) designated certain communities as 'born criminals' — the Pasi community's classification under this Act made Madari Pasi's public leadership an act of political defiance on multiple levels.
• Post-independence, the Criminal Tribes Act was repealed in 1952 and replaced with the Habitual Offenders Act — a partial reform.
• The Pasi community of UP later became an important constituency in caste-based electoral politics, with leaders like Ram Vilas Paswan tracing their political heritage to such historically marginalised communities.

solution.concept_anchor: Geographical localisation of Eka vs. geographic diffusion of Mappila

statement_analysis.statement: The Eka movement remained confined to three districts of the Awadh region — Hardoi, Bahraich, and Sitapur — and never achieved state-wide or national territorial expansion.
statement_analysis.reason: The Eka movement's localisation to these three districts is a defining characteristic — it never spread to other UP districts or achieved pan-UP or national scale despite the universality of agrarian grievances.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mappila Rebellion of 1921 was geographically centred in the Malabar region of what is now Kerala, distinguishing it from the Awadh-based Eka movement in terms of both location and the specific tenurial grievances involved.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mappila Rebellion was indeed in Malabar (present-day Kerala's northern region) — a geographically distinct theatre with a different tenurial structure (Muslim tenant-peasants under predominantly Hindu Janmi landlords), correctly contrasting with Awadh's taluqdari system.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the Eka movement, the Mappila Rebellion spread rapidly from Malabar across the entire Madras Presidency and eventually reached Bombay Presidency, making it a pan-South Indian agrarian movement.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mappila Rebellion was also geographically localised — it was confined to Malabar district of the Madras Presidency. It did not spread across the Madras Presidency or reach Bombay. The statement exaggerates its geographic diffusion.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that the Mappila Rebellion had significant historical impact may incorrectly accept its geographic reach as pan-South Indian, making them reluctant to mark Statement 3 as NOT correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Eka's confinement to three districts is a documented fact.
Statement 2 is correct — Mappila Rebellion's Malabar location is accurate.
Statement 3 is NOT correct — the Mappila Rebellion was also geographically localised to Malabar; it did not spread across the Madras Presidency or reach Bombay.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — answer is (d) '3 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in Statement 3 exaggerates the Mappila Rebellion's geographic reach. Students who know it was a significant movement with national-level political impact (it embarrassed the Congress-Khilafat alliance) may conflate historical significance with territorial reach. The Mappila Rebellion was intense within Malabar but did not spread to other regions — its significance was political and symbolic, not territorial. Confusing the movement's national political resonance with geographic diffusion is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Both the Eka movement and the Mappila Rebellion exemplify the principle that historically significant agrarian movements can be geographically highly localised — their importance lies in what they reveal about colonial agrarian structures, not in territorial reach.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Eka's confinement to Hardoi, Bahraich, and Sitapur is both a historical fact and a significant analytical point about the limitations of informal oath-based mobilisation in achieving regional scale.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Mappila Rebellion was centred in Malabar (present-day northern Kerala) — a distinct tenurial theatre with Muslim sharecroppers and Hindu Janmi landlords, different from Awadh's multi-layer taluqdari structure.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Mappila Rebellion, like Eka, was geographically localised — to Malabar district. It did not spread across the Madras Presidency or reach Bombay. Its national significance derived from its political implications for the Congress-Khilafat alliance, not from geographic expansion.

Value Addition:
• The Ernad and Valluvanad taluks within Malabar were the specific epicentres of Mappila violence in 1921 — a level of geographic precision comparable to Eka's three-district focus.
• Geographic localisation of agrarian movements is a recurring feature of colonial India — the Deccan Riots (1875) were similarly confined to specific taluks of Pune and Ahmednagar districts.
• The contrast between geographic localisation and national political impact is an important analytical tool for understanding peasant movements — local intensity can have national consequences through political reverberations.

solution.concept_anchor: Begar resistance — Eka vs. Kumaon comparison and women's role

statement_analysis.statement: Begar in the Awadh context included unpaid labour services for zamindars spanning agricultural tasks like harvesting, construction activities, and domestic service — all extracted through social coercion without explicit legal authorisation.
statement_analysis.reason: The comprehensive forms of begar in Awadh — agricultural, construction, and domestic — extracted without explicit legal authorisation through social coercion is accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: The Eka movement's pledge to refuse begar was operationally identical to the Gandhian begar resistance in the Kumaon hills (1921), both movements being directed by the Indian National Congress through the same Non-Cooperation framework.
statement_analysis.reason: While both resisted begar in 1921, the Eka movement was not directed by Congress through the Non-Cooperation framework — it maintained organisational independence. The Kumaon resistance had more direct Gandhian-Congress involvement; Eka used the oath mechanism autonomously.

statement_analysis.statement: Lower-caste women in the Eka movement participated in oath assemblies and served as household and village enforcers of the collective begar-refusal pledge, though they held no formal leadership positions.
statement_analysis.reason: Women's dual role — public oath-assembly participation and informal enforcement within households/villages — combined with their exclusion from formal leadership is accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: The legal ambiguity of begar — neither explicitly authorised nor explicitly prohibited by colonial statute — made legal resistance to it more complex than resistance to nazrana, which had been formally prohibited by colonial tenancy law.
statement_analysis.reason: Nazrana was also not formally prohibited by colonial tenancy law — it was simply unrecognised (extra-legal), not explicitly banned. Both begar and nazrana occupied similar legal grey zones; nazrana was not 'formally prohibited' any more than begar was.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may count Statements 1, 2, and 3 as correct (accepting the false equivalence with Kumaon), arriving at 'Only three.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the forms and legal status of begar in Awadh are accurately described.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Eka was not directed by Congress through Non-Cooperation; it was autonomous. The 'operationally identical' and 'directed by Congress' elements falsify this statement.
Statement 3 is correct — women's participation in oath assemblies and their informal enforcement role without formal leadership is accurately described.

Statement 4 is incorrect — nazrana was also extra-legal (not formally prohibited), not formally banned by colonial tenancy law. The parallel legal status of begar and nazrana makes the comparative claim in Statement 4 false.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is a subtle partial-truth trap. The statement's claim about nazrana being 'formally prohibited' seems plausible because students know Eka targeted nazrana as illegal — but extra-legal and formally prohibited are different things. The same legal ambiguity that characterised begar also characterised nazrana. Students who correctly understand begar's legal grey zone but have not applied the same analysis to nazrana will accept Statement 4's false comparison. Statement 2's 'operationally identical' claim is a simpler conflation that well-prepared students should catch.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the distinct forms of agrarian exploitation and the legal framework surrounding them is essential for precise analysis of Eka's demands.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Begar in Awadh encompassed agricultural, construction, and domestic unpaid labour — all extracted through social coercion without explicit statutory authorisation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Eka and Kumaon begar resistances were contemporaneous (1921) but organisationally and methodologically distinct. Eka used oath-assemblies autonomously without Congress direction; the Kumaon resistance had more direct Gandhian involvement. Calling them 'operationally identical' and 'directed by Congress through the same framework' is doubly false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Women's public participation in oath assemblies and their role as informal household/village enforcers of collective pledges — without formal leadership — is accurately described.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Both begar and nazrana occupied the same legal grey zone — extra-legal (not formally authorised) rather than formally prohibited by statute. Nazrana was NOT formally banned by colonial tenancy law, which is precisely why Eka's refusal required the oath mechanism rather than legal appeals.

Value Addition:
• The Kumaon begar resistance (1921) is associated with Badri Datt Pandey and had more direct Gandhi-Congress structural involvement than Eka — a comparative fact useful for distinguishing these two 1921 begar-resistance movements.
• The overlap between begar and nazrana as extra-legal exactions reflects the broader pattern of colonial law tolerating informal exploitation while maintaining formal legal neutrality.
• Women's participation in Eka oath assemblies challenged the purdah norms of upper-caste communities — demonstrating how lower-caste social mobility restrictions (poverty rather than purdah) paradoxically enabled greater public participation.

solution.concept_anchor: Eka movement — class contradiction within Indian nationalism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may correctly identify both A and R as true but be uncertain whether R genuinely explains A — the causal link (Congress's multi-class coalition character → reluctance to support radical agrarian movements → class contradiction exposed) is real but requires two inferential steps.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Eka movement's experience — where Congress deliberately kept distance from radical lower-caste agrarian mobilisation to protect its propertied-class support base — exposed the class contradiction within Indian nationalism: a movement claiming to represent 'the people' but protecting zamindars against lower-caste peasants.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Congress's multi-class coalition included zamindars and taluqdars as significant supporters, and Congress feared alienating these classes by endorsing radical anti-zamindar peasant movements.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. R (Congress's multi-class coalition character and consequent reluctance to alienate propertied classes) is precisely the mechanism that produced the class contradiction described in A. Congress's class caution IS the class contradiction — R explains the specific form it took.
Both A and R are correct, R explains A — answer is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Eka movement's most lasting contribution to Indian political history may be its role in forcing a confrontation with the class contradictions embedded within Indian nationalism.

• Assertion (A): Correct. When Congress kept deliberate distance from the Eka movement — a lower-caste tenant uprising against zamindars — it revealed that the nationalist coalition's proclaimed unity masked significant class conflicts. 'The people' whose freedom was sought included both exploiting zamindars and exploited lower-caste peasants.
• Reason (R): Correct. Congress's coalition structure included zamindars and taluqdars as major local organisational supporters and financiers in UP — men like Motilal Nehru represented this propertied class within the Congress. Supporting Eka against zamindars would have fractured this coalition.
• Causal relationship: R correctly explains A. Congress's multi-class coalition character — requiring it to balance propertied and labouring class interests — is precisely the mechanism that produced the class contradiction exposed by Eka. The contradiction was not accidental but structural, rooted in Congress's political sociology.

Value Addition:
• This class contradiction persisted and was not resolved until Jawaharlal Nehru's more explicit agrarian reform commitments in the 1930s–40s, eventually leading to zamindari abolition legislation in the 1950s.
• The Eka movement was not unique in exposing this contradiction — the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) also raised questions about whose interests Congress's agrarian mobilisations ultimately served.
• Marxist historians have used the Congress-Eka distance as evidence that the nationalist movement was not a vehicle of peasant liberation but of bourgeois-landlord class consolidation — a position that overstates the case but captures a real dynamic.

solution.concept_anchor: Awadh tenurial system — comparative colonial settlements
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may conflate the Permanent Settlement (Bengal) with Awadh's post-1856 structure because both created zamindars as revenue intermediaries, leading them to match A with '1' and then be forced into incorrect secondary matches.
elimination_logic: Match A (Awadh post-1856 settlement): Created taluqdars as loyal intermediaries through political engineering after annexation — links to '3' (re-engineered to create a loyalist taluqdari class).

Match B (Permanent Settlement 1793): Created zamindars as hereditary revenue payers in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa with fixed revenue liability — links to '4' (fixed revenue liability with zamindars as permanent revenue settlement).
Match C (Ryotwari Settlement): Direct revenue relationship between cultivating peasant and colonial state, no intermediaries — links to '1' (direct state-cultivator revenue relationship).
Match D (Mahalwari Settlement): Revenue settled with village communities (mahals) collectively in North-Western Provinces — links to '2' (village community as the unit of revenue settlement).
Correct matching: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the Permanent Settlement's zamindari creation with Awadh's taluqdari creation — both created intermediary revenue-collecting classes, but through different mechanisms and with different political logic. The Permanent Settlement (1793) was a revenue certainty measure; Awadh's post-1856 settlement was political consolidation after annexation. Students who see 'zamindar/taluqdar as intermediary' as the common description may match both A and B to the same description. The specific phrases 'loyalist taluqdari class' (political motivation) and 'fixed revenue liability' (revenue certainty motivation) distinguish the two.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the different land revenue settlement systems is essential for contextualising peasant movements — each system created different class structures and different forms of exploitation.

• A–3: Awadh's post-1856 settlement deliberately created a loyalist taluqdari class through political engineering — rewarding loyal taluqdars after the 1857 rebellion to consolidate British control. This political motivation distinguishes it from purely revenue-driven settlements.
• B–4: The Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa fixed revenue liability in perpetuity with zamindars — a revenue certainty measure that created hereditary property rights in zamindars regardless of agricultural performance.
• C–1: The Ryotwari Settlement (Madras, Bombay Presidencies) established direct revenue relationships between individual cultivating peasants (ryots) and the colonial state — the only system with no intermediary revenue layer.
• D–2: The Mahalwari Settlement (North-Western Provinces, Punjab) used the village community (mahal) collectively as the unit of revenue settlement — creating joint village responsibility for revenue payment.

Value Addition:
• The Permanent Settlement's fixed revenue meant zamindars kept all productivity gains — a strong incentive to extract maximum rent from tenants, leading to sub-infeudation.
• Awadh's taluqdari system had sub-infeudation even more acute than Bengal — the mahajan-zamindar-taluqdar chain created multiple extraction layers above the cultivating peasant.
• UPSC frequently tests which settlement system applied to which region — Ryotwari (South India), Permanent Settlement (Bengal), Mahalwari (North India), Awadh taluqdari (post-1856) are the four distinct systems to know.

solution.concept_anchor: Eka movement immediate triggers — rent levels and timing

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: At the time of the Eka movement's emergence, rents in the affected Awadh districts were being collected at rates approximately 50% above those recorded in official settlement documents — a gap that made Eka's demand for recorded-rate rent payment a substantive economic challenge to zamindar income.
statement_analysis.reason: The 50% above recorded rate figure is the documented magnitude of excess rent extraction in the Hardoi-Bahraich-Sitapur districts — this gap is what made Eka's demand both legally defensible and economically significant.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The post-World War I economic boom in India provided most rural communities with rising incomes that insulated Awadh peasants from agrarian distress, meaning the Eka movement arose despite general prosperity rather than economic hardship.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-WWI India experienced inflationary pressures and agrarian distress — not prosperity for rural communities. Prices rose sharply but peasant incomes did not keep pace, worsening the gap between rent burdens and productive capacity. The Eka movement arose precisely because of post-WWI economic distress, not despite prosperity.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate the 'post-WWI' period with industrialisation and economic activity may incorrectly accept Statement 2's prosperity claim, leading them to select (a) both correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 50% above recorded rate is the precise documented figure for excess rent in Awadh's Eka districts — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Post-WWI India experienced inflationary prices and agrarian distress — not rural prosperity. Peasant real incomes fell while rent burdens remained or increased. Statement 2's 'general prosperity' claim is the opposite of the historical record — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 2 exploits ambiguity about the post-WWI economic situation. Students who associate WWI with wartime industrial demand and economic activity may project a prosperity narrative onto the post-war period for India. In reality, the post-WWI period brought inflationary pressure on consumer goods while peasant incomes stagnated — a standard feature of agrarian distress that fed peasant movements across India in 1919–22. The statement deliberately uses 'economic boom' to activate this temporal confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The triggers of the Eka movement operated at two levels — the specific economic mechanism of excess rent extraction and the broader context of post-WWI agrarian distress.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rents in Awadh's Eka districts were collected at approximately 50% above recorded rates — the gap between legal obligation and actual extraction is documented and formed the economic basis for Eka's demand for recorded-rate-only payment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Post-WWI India experienced the opposite of rural prosperity. Inflationary prices for consumer goods squeezed rural households while zamindars maintained or increased rent demands. This post-war economic distress was a major structural cause of peasant mobilisation across India in 1919–22 — including Eka, the Kisan Sabha movement, and the Mappila Rebellion.

Value Addition:
• Post-WWI inflation in India was partly a consequence of war financing — the colonial government raised money through bonds and expenditure that created inflationary pressure.
• The 1918–19 influenza pandemic ('Spanish flu') further devastated rural communities in India, compounding post-war economic distress and contributing to the peasant mobilisation wave of 1919–22.
• The 50% excess rent figure in Awadh contrasts with the Champaran case (indigo cultivation compulsory on 3/20 of land — the 'tinkathia' system) — different specific mechanisms but the same pattern of excess extraction beyond legal limits.

solution.concept_anchor: Colonial suppression — class-caste bias in administration's response
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Gandhi-led movements also faced colonial repression may assume the colonial response was equally brutal across all anti-colonial movements, making option (a) 'equally brutal across all movements' seem plausible — but the historical evidence shows differential treatment based on the social profile of the movement.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — colonial response was NOT uniform across movements. Gandhi-led campaigns received more negotiated responses (Round Table Conferences, Gandhi-Irwin Pact) while lower-caste peasant uprisings received direct military-police suppression without negotiation.
Eliminate option (c) — the colonial government did not negotiate rent concessions with Eka leaders; it suppressed the movement through arrests and military deployment.
Eliminate option (d) — the colonial government did not request Congress to resolve the Eka agitation; it dealt with Eka through direct repression.

Option (b) correctly identifies the differential colonial response: more brutal, less negotiated repression of lower-caste peasant movements compared to elite nationalist campaigns — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (a) generalises colonial repression uniformly across all anti-colonial movements. Students who know colonialism was repressive overall may accept this as accurate. The critical nuance is that the colonial administration's response was calibrated by the social class of the movement's leadership and participants — movements led by upper-class educated nationalists received more negotiated treatment than lower-caste peasant uprisings. This differential treatment reflects both race and class biases within colonial administration.
solution.final_explanation:
The British colonial response to the Eka movement was characterised by direct military and police repression without the negotiated response that Gandhi-led movements sometimes received.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Colonial repression was NOT uniform. The colonial administration negotiated with Gandhi-led campaigns (Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931, Round Table Conferences) in ways it never considered for lower-caste peasant movements like Eka — which received immediate police and military suppression.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Eka movement faced more brutal, less negotiated suppression than Gandhi-led movements — a differential response reflecting the colonial administration's class and caste bias. Lower-caste peasant assemblies were treated as seditious threats; elite nationalist protests were managed through negotiation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There were no rent concession negotiations between colonial authorities and Eka leaders. The government's response was arrest of Madari Pasi and dispersal of oath assemblies through the Seditious Meetings Act.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The colonial government did not ask Congress to intermediate with Eka — it directly suppressed the movement. Congress had no leverage over Eka anyway, given the movement's deliberate independence from Congress.

Value Addition:
• The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) exemplifies negotiated colonial response to elite nationalist campaigns — a level of political recognition never extended to lower-caste agrarian movements.
• Colonial administration's differential treatment of 'political' and 'criminal' movements tracked closely with the social class of the movements' leadership — a structural bias documented in official correspondence.
• Mass arrests of Eka participants extended beyond Madari Pasi to hundreds of lower-level oath-assembly participants — a dragnet approach not typically used against Congress political workers.

solution.concept_anchor: Eka movement demands vs. demands of other agrarian movements
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Tebhaga movement demanded two-thirds of the harvest may think this is a more 'radical' demand unlike Eka's moderate position — but Tebhaga was still a demand-based (not abolition-based) tenant movement, similar in type to Eka's demand-based approach. The odd one out is zamindari abolition.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: All three correct items should be specific agrarian demands articulated by lower-caste or tenant-peasant movements (not structural abolition demands).
'Refusal to pay nazrana' — a specific Eka demand against extra-legal payments.
'Two-thirds crop share for sharecroppers' (Tebhaga demand) — a specific redistributive demand within the existing tenurial framework.
'Right to pasture lands' — a specific Eka demand for resource access.

'Abolition of the zamindari system' — a structural demand for elimination of the entire tenurial class, associated with post-independence legislative programmes and later radical movements, not Eka's moderate demand-based resistance.
The odd one out is 'Abolition of the zamindari system' — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges demands of different historical periods and movement types. Students who know the zamindari system was eventually abolished may associate zamindari abolition with the peasant movement tradition that includes Eka. But Eka explicitly did NOT demand zamindari abolition — its demands were for specific legal-rent-rights within the existing tenurial framework. Zamindari abolition was a legislative demand of independent India's agrarian reform programme (UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950) — decades after Eka.
solution.final_explanation:
The Eka movement was characterised by deliberately moderate demands — specific, legally defensible resistance to illegal exactions within the existing tenurial framework, not structural transformation.

• 'Refusal to pay nazrana' — belongs to the set: a core Eka demand targeting the extra-legal premium above recorded rent.
• 'Right to pasture lands' — belongs to the set: a specific Eka demand for access to common resource lands that zamindars had appropriated.
• 'Two-thirds crop share for sharecroppers' — belongs to the set: this is the Tebhaga movement's (1946–47) specific redistributive demand, but it is still a specific tenant-rights demand within an existing agrarian framework rather than structural abolition.
• 'Abolition of the zamindari system' — DOES NOT belong: this is a structural demand for elimination of the entire intermediary tenure class. The Eka movement explicitly did not make this demand. Zamindari abolition was associated with post-independence legislation and with more radical movements like Telangana — not with Eka's moderate, legally-framed resistance strategy.

Value Addition:
• The UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act (1950) was among the first state laws passed in independent India — a legislative fulfilment of demands that movements like Eka's era never articulated but whose exposure of zamindari exploitation contributed to.
• Eka's moderation was strategic: by staying within the legal framework ('pay recorded rent, refuse illegal extras'), it positioned itself as law-abiding and zamindars as the violators.
• The contrast between Eka's moderate demands and Telangana's armed agrarian revolution (1946–51) illustrates the full spectrum of peasant movement ideological orientations in India.

solution.concept_anchor: Nationalist historiography — subsumption of Eka under Non-Cooperation

statement_analysis.statement: Nationalist historiography, by treating the Eka movement as a constituent part of the Non-Cooperation Movement, effectively erases the movement's organisational independence, lower-caste social character, and its challenge to upper-caste Congress leadership.
statement_analysis.reason: This precisely describes the Subaltern Studies critique of nationalist historiography — the subsumption of Eka into the Non-Cooperation narrative is identified as the primary distortion, one that erases Eka's autonomous lower-caste character.

statement_analysis.statement: Gyanendra Pandey's recovery of the Eka movement within the Subaltern Studies tradition treats peasant consciousness as fully autonomous and entirely independent of all external influences including nationalist politics and colonial administrative events.
statement_analysis.reason: Subaltern Studies recovers peasant consciousness as autonomous and irreducible to elite agendas — but not as 'entirely independent of all external influences.' The Subaltern approach acknowledges interactions with nationalist and colonial contexts while insisting that subaltern agency cannot be reduced to those contexts. 'Entirely independent of all external influences' is an overstatement that the Subaltern approach itself would reject.

statement_analysis.statement: The Marxist historiographical approach to the Eka movement recognises its class potential while identifying its religious idiom and organisational informality as constraints that prevented it from developing into a fully revolutionary agrarian movement.
statement_analysis.reason: The Marxist interpretation characterises Eka as having incipient class-struggle potential that was constrained by religious idiom and lack of revolutionary organisation — this is precisely the Marxist assessment of the movement.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who partially understand the Subaltern Studies approach may accept Statement 2's 'entirely autonomous' description as consistent with subaltern theory — Subaltern Studies does emphasise autonomy, but not complete isolation from all external influences.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the nationalist historiography critique regarding subsumption of Eka is accurately described.

Statement 2 is incorrect — 'entirely independent of all external influences' overstates the Subaltern Studies position; the approach claims peasant agency cannot be reduced to elite agendas, not that it was isolated from all external context.
Statement 3 is correct — the Marxist assessment of Eka as incipient class struggle constrained by religious idiom is accurately described.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's partial-truth trap lies in the phrase 'entirely independent of all external influences.' Students who know Subaltern Studies emphasises subaltern autonomy may accept this as a natural extension of the Subaltern position. The distinction is crucial: Subaltern Studies argues that subaltern consciousness cannot be reduced to elite nationalist agendas — not that it operates in complete isolation from colonial, nationalist, or economic contexts. The word 'entirely' is the falsification point, converting a nuanced methodological claim into an absolute that the approach itself does not make.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing what different historiographical schools actually claim about the Eka movement — rather than what they might be expected to claim — is essential for this question.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nationalist historiography's subsumption of Eka under Non-Cooperation erases three crucial dimensions: organisational independence, lower-caste social character, and the challenge to upper-caste Congress leadership. All three erasures are identified in Subaltern Studies critiques.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Subaltern Studies approach claims peasant consciousness has its own internal logic irreducible to elite nationalist agendas — not that it was 'entirely independent of all external influences.' Subaltern scholars fully acknowledge interactions between peasant movements and nationalist politics; they merely insist these interactions do not explain away subaltern agency.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Marxist assessment of Eka as incipient class struggle constrained by religious idiom and lack of revolutionary organisation is a standard characterisation across Marxist historical scholarship on colonial-era peasant movements.

Value Addition:
• The debate between Subaltern Studies and Marxist approaches centres on whether religious idiom represents 'false consciousness' (Marxist view) or an autonomous cultural logic (Subaltern view).
• Ranajit Guha's concept of 'elementary aspects of peasant insurgency' — including negation, ambiguity, solidarity, and transmission — provides a framework for analysing Eka that goes beyond simple class or nationalist categories.
• For UPSC purposes: nationalist = subsumes into Non-Cooperation; Marxist = incipient class struggle, constrained by religion; Subaltern = autonomous agency irreducible to elite agendas.

solution.concept_anchor: Eka movement in broader 1920–22 political chronology
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may place the Nagpur Congress session after Chauri Chaura because they associate both with the 'later Non-Cooperation period,' reversing the Nagpur and Chauri Chaura positions.
elimination_logic: Nagpur Congress session (December 1920) adopted the Non-Cooperation resolution — this is the earliest event, establishing the national framework.
Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920) was established in the same year — can be placed contemporaneously or just after Nagpur in the agrarian mobilisation sequence.
The Eka movement emerged in late 1921 — after the Kisan Sabha had already been operating.
Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922) is the final event — the external shock that led to Non-Cooperation's suspension.
Correct order: Nagpur Congress session → Awadh Kisan Sabha → Eka movement emergence → Chauri Chaura — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap primarily targets students who conflate the Nagpur Congress session's timing with later Non-Cooperation events. Nagpur (December 1920) is earlier than most students intuitively place it — they may associate 'Nagpur' with the 1923 Congress or other sessions. The correct identification of December 1920 as the Nagpur Non-Cooperation resolution session is the anchor for the entire chronological sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The correct chronological sequence reveals the causal chain of Awadh agrarian politics within the broader Non-Cooperation Movement context.

• Nagpur Congress session (December 1920): The Indian National Congress adopted the Non-Cooperation resolution at Nagpur — creating the national political atmosphere that gave energy to allied peasant mobilisations.
• Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920): Established under Baba Ramchandra in the same period, drawing on the Non-Cooperation energy but with its own agrarian agenda — the immediate organisational precursor to Eka.
• Eka movement emergence (late 1921): As the Kisan Sabha's upper-peasant limitations became apparent and agrarian grievances persisted despite the Oudh Rent Amendment Act, Madari Pasi organised the lower-caste oath-assemblies.
• Chauri Chaura incident (4 February 1922): The burning of the police station and killing of 22 policemen led Gandhi to suspend Non-Cooperation, demoralising allied peasant activism and contributing to Eka's eventual collapse.

Value Addition:
• The Nagpur session (1920) is also notable for adopting a new Congress constitution that reorganised provincial Congress committees on linguistic lines — a significant internal restructuring.
• The Chauri Chaura police station burning was not directly connected to Eka — it was in Gorakhpur district, separate from Eka's three districts — but its political consequences affected all peasant movements.
• The 20-month window between Nagpur (December 1920) and Chauri Chaura (February 1922) encapsulates the entire active phase of the Non-Cooperation Movement — and of the Eka movement.

solution.concept_anchor: Eka oath strategy — legal defensibility through recorded-rate compliance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may interpret the oath-assemblies as a form of civil disobedience similar to Gandhi's satyagraha and choose 'complete non-payment of rent' as the strategy, confusing Eka's moderate legal-compliance approach with outright rent non-payment.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a strategy that is legally defensible — this eliminates outright rent non-payment (which would be a clear breach of tenancy law).
The scenario's key element is framing resistance within existing legal frameworks — targeting the gap between legal obligation and actual extraction.

Eka's approach was specifically: pay what the law says (recorded rent), refuse what the law does not authorise (nazrana, begar) — this makes resistance legally defensible and positions zamindars as the violators.
Option (c) — paying only the legally recorded rent and publicly refusing extra-legal exactions — is the correct application of Eka's strategic principle.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests understanding of the Eka movement's central strategic insight — that legally defensible resistance is more powerful than resistance that can be criminalised.

The Eka movement's genius was that it did not call for breaking the law but for enforcing it. By pledging to pay rent at recorded rates and nothing more, Eka peasants were exercising their legal entitlements. Zamindars who demanded more were the ones operating outside the law. This framing made colonial authorities' task more complex — they could not easily criminalise compliance with legal obligations.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Complete non-payment of rent was never Eka's strategy. That would have made Eka participants clear-cut legal violators and given colonial authorities easy grounds for prosecution. Eka's moderation was strategic, not a limitation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Appealing to colonial courts individually was neither practical for illiterate rural communities nor Eka's collective resistance method. Individual court cases require resources and time that peasants lacked.
• Option (c) — Correct: Paying only the recorded rent while publicly pledging to refuse nazrana, begar, and arbitrary eviction compliance was Eka's precise strategy — legally defensible collective resistance.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Seeking Congress mediation contradicts Eka's organisational independence from Congress. Eka deliberately did not subordinate itself to Congress frameworks.

Value Addition:
• This 'legal compliance as resistance' strategy was also used in the Champaran Satyagraha — Gandhi insisted peasants were merely asserting their legal rights against the tinkathia system.
• The strategic value of keeping resistance within legal bounds is that it forces authorities to either change the law or reveal the gap between law and actual administration — both outcomes unfavourable to the colonial system.
• The Eka oath's sacred and binding character served as the collective enforcement mechanism that made individual legal compliance into collective political resistance.
